For more details, here's the Show HN post:

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49937916

From the comments, I got the impression that there was quite an interest in seeing not only AI-generated LEGO models, but also AI-animated LEGO ones.

I took a look at results from past experiments, and found it feasible to use agentic LLMs for:

- analyzing the LDraw source code for LEGO models\n- reverse-engineer! the mechanisms present by reading the descriptions and sequence for the parts there\n- and then, animate them via Blender!

This new project I'm presenting, LDraw Mecha, is the end result and proof that can be done:

- Read specially annotated LDraw LEGO models .mpd source files\n- Infer the model structure in terms of submodels\n- Select from those the ones that are mechanisms\n- Plan animations\n- Execute them in Blender

In summary, from an initial .mpd source file, get a rigged and animated version for the model as a Blender (.blend) file.

See the results here:

- Repo (v0.5.0): https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/tree/v0.5.0\n- Gallery: https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/GALLERY.m...\n- Process: https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/PROCESS.m...

Waymark\u2019s an open source durable execution library with similar functionality to Temporal or DBOS.

I fell in love with durable execution a few years ago, after working at a company with a heavy pubsub architecture. In comparison to job orchestrators that force a certain task design or special syntax, many of these durable libs lets you write business logic in regular code: `asyncio.gather` to parallelize tasks, `for` loops, conditionals, and let the runtime figure out how to distribute them efficiently across a cluster of nodes. But most of the current solutions require a heavy broker, runtime hacks to try to ensure deterministic implementation of workflow logic, and feel like you have to learn a whole new ecosystem just to get started.

A few unique design decisions in waymark:

\u2014 Write jobs in normal code (right now Python but JS coming soon). Instead of running control flow as-is, which requires booting up an interpreter to replay past state, we\u2019ll just compile your code directly. We walk your AST and map your logic to our stackless VM bytecode. We support variables, conditionals, await, sleep, helper functions, loops... basically what you\u2019d expect in workflow logic.

\u2014 Since we\u2019re compiling a language subset, we can proactively flag errors in your workflows locally instead of when they run in production.

\u2014 It only requires Postgres as the task broker. We\u2019ve spent a lot of time tuning our design to play nicely with its strengths and limitations; our current benchmarks show around 1500 workflows/second but we still have some more optimization work to do here.

\u2014 Actions plug-and-play with FastAPI\u2019s dependency injection syntax. So if you already have an ecosystem based on typehinting/DI, it should fit like a glove.

It allows for parallelization of workflows across one machine or a whole cluster. The bulk of the work per node is done by our central Rust core - which distributes workflows to properly saturate all cores. The idea is to be as batteries included as possible with the broker, webapp, and runtime.

What to use it for? It works great as the runner loop controlling agents, but it also works well for basically any task that you need to kick off in the background. It\u2019s largely replaced our way of writing api code. Most frontend actions at this point just push to a simple REST endpoint that kick off a background job.

I spent an embarrassing amount of time making our https://waymark.sh site interactive - it\u2019s probably the best place to learn more. We\u2019re starting with Python support and looking for community input on what language to ship next. This is something so many people don't realize.

When you hold your breath for too long, that feeling of suffocation isn't caused by a lack of oxygen, but the build-up of CO2.

If you replace the oxygen in a room with an odorless gas non-oxygen gas, your body doesn't tell you. You don't feel like you're suffocating. You just start suffering the effects of lack of oxygen. Dizziness, confusion, lightheadedness, but you likely won't realize anything is wrong. Your judgement and ability to react goes away and you lose consciousness without ever experiencing the desperate urge to breathe.

Another good example of this is when pilots fly too high without supplemental oxygen or adequate cabin pressurization and become hypoxic. They become confused and lose coordination while feeling perfectly fine. Plus, in the midwest, the ranges tank in the dead of winter, due to sub-zero temperatures and headwinds.","title":null,"type":"comment","url":null}],"created_at":"2026-11-06T15:27:03.000Z","created_at_i":1793978823,"id":50393496,"options":[],"parent_id":50393177,"points":null,"story_id":50391456,"text":"Not that I am trying to argue with you, I'm not, but people have a "gas station mindset" about EVs and it leads to confusion, so let me spell out how this trip would look with a "charging station" mindset:

Leave home at 100%/200mi

Drive to destination (approx 3 hours) arrive with ~0%/0mi

Charge while at destination to 80%/160mi

Begin driving back home with a 20%/40mi deficit of range.

Stop anywhere/anytime after you get below 60%/120mi

Charge for 20%/40mi (~10 minutes)

Complete drive home and fully charge again.

Total extra time on 400 mile trip vs gas (assuming 300 mi tank range, so 1 fill-up): ~5 minutes (or 8 minutes if you stop for a quick charge on the way so you don't have to white knuckle down to 0%).

For cold driving in the winter, it would probably be closer to an extra 20 minutes.","title":null,"type":"comment","url":null}],"created_at":"2026-11-06T15:03:13.000Z","created_at_i":1793977393,"id":50393177,"options":[],"parent_id":50392909,"points":null,"story_id":50391456,"text":"Personally I live in the Midwest. I should've been more specific. The 1980s and 1990s Hilux weighed in at 1000-1200kg. Now it's 1700-2100kg. It's a lot bigger truck. Those 1980s and 1990s trucks were indestructible and so easy to service.

Now I get why the gas powered Hilux has changed. Emissions standards have changed. Fuel efficiency is more important. Modern cars are full of computers and microcontrollers. But an EV is relatively simple. It's one of the big advantages. Yes you have an OS and it's not just turning the ignition but the drive system itself is fairly simple, the thing that turns battery power into movement (compared to ICEs). No moving parts (in the engine), basically.

You could absolutely make a small EV utility truck. Remember that part of the reason why people were excited about the Cybertruck when it was announced was the price point (~$35k). Of course it turned out to be 3 times that.

Look at what BYD is doing [1]. Now these are PHEVs rather than pure EVs. Other automakers are making smaller pure EV trucks.

This is a very common misconception Americans believe about the hilux. I\u2019ve owned multiple generations of both on different continents.

The Tacoma is much heavier, but has a much lower payload rating. It has way less torque, and gets much worse fuel economy. The Tacoma only comes with a regular bed- no cab chassis, no tray back, etc.

The Tacoma is much more expensive. The Tacoma only exists in two countries. The hilux is one of only a few truly global vehicles.

One is a genuine work utility vehicle, one is a lifestyle vehicle.

They have never shared a frame, engine, transmission, axles or body panels.

A Tacoma is basically the US model of the Hilux.","title":null,"type":"comment","url":null}],"created_at":"2026-11-06T14:14:22.000Z","created_at_i":1793974462,"id":50392513,"options":[],"parent_id":50391456,"points":null,"story_id":50391456,"text":"Behold the Toyota Hilux [1], a truck so reliable that it is the truck of choice in many developed nations and even less developed ones. It's so cheap and reliable it became the platform for a war [2]. It also has a truck bed equivalent to a Ford F150, a vehicle significantly larger. But you can't buy a new Hilux or equivalent in the US because cars younger than 25 years cannot legally be imported [3] (to stop grey imports on Mercedes in the 1980s, originally) and because of CAFE standards [4].

Electric vehicles obviously don't have the hurdle of meeting emissions standards so Tesla, or any other company really, had (and has) the opportunity to create a small, cheap, mass market utility truck that no gas-powered vehicle can compete with. This is what the Cybertruck should've been.

There have been breakdowns of the Cybertruck and it is such an incredibly bad design. Things like the weight of stainless steel panels but with an aluminum frame. Why is that a problem? Because aluminum is prone to catastrophic failure with the up and down motion of towing a heavy load than stainless steel simply isn't [5].

The rumor has been that the only thing propping up Cybertruck demand is Elon forcing his own companies like SpaceX to buy them [6]. Other than that, the Cybertruck became a weird political statement [7]. Those people are getting crucified on resale. It's even a trend on Tiktok and elsewhere to watch these trade in videos. People who paid $150k+ are getting <$70k less than 2 years later.

Anyway, I'm shocked no US manufacturer is tackling the EV small utility truck market. Yes there was the F150 Lightning but it's still too big (and thus expensive).

The total acceleration comes from the initial difference in speed between the two things that collide and the proportion of the acceleration applied to each object is inversely proportional to their relative masses.

If they have the same mass then they each take half. If one of them is 19 times heavier then the other one takes 95% of the acceleration. If one of them is six hundred trillion times heavier then the other one takes ~100% of the acceleration, but this is still only ~5% more than taking 95%.

Consider what happens if you walk at 2 MPH into a concrete pillar which is fully anchored into the Earth. The mass of the Earth makes the mass of your body look like zero with some zeros after it, so are you immediately crushed? Simpler gas equipment like mowers and generators don't have enough compression to really care about anything but ancient gas, and if you run any vehicle that is multi-fuel capable it can detect and adjust compression based on a fuel's capabilities.

Ive been repairing and fixing junkers of cars, mowers, ATVs, generators, and more for 30 years and not once has bad gas stopped something from running. The thing is that ICE vehicles are so inefficient to begin with, but a towed trailer needs the same amount of energy regardless of what is towing it.\nImagine a trailer takes 1 unit of energy to move, and ICE truck takes 5 units to move itself, and EV truck takes 1 unit to move itself.
